newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Local demand keeps Indonesia cocoa prices steady.
newsitem.headline: Local demand keeps Indonesia cocoa prices steady.

text.p: Indonesia's secondary cocoa harvest has got off to a slow start and traders are offering unprecedented incentives to secure supplies, industry sources said on Wednesday.

They said farmers, using satellite dishes tuned to financial television channels, were keeping a close watch on developments in key markets such as New York and London as they bargained for better prices.
"The market is becoming fiercely competitive," one trader based in Ujung Pandang, capital of the growing region of South Sulawesi, told Reuters by telephone.
"They (farmers) can tell us by how many points prices at the New York terminal rose and how much they should get for their beans," the trader with a leading trading house said.

Traders said the competition to secure supplies had led one trading firm to offer farmers a fixed range of prices for four consecutive days on the assurance that even if prices fell below the offered levels, the contracts would be honoured.
If prices rose, the trading firm had guaranteed it would honour the higher price, they said.
"It is very risky," one trader said. "I wouldn't do it."
Traders said the slow start to the mid-crop harvest was keeping prices steady at 2,750 rupiah ($1.19) per kg (2.2 lbs) in Ujung Pandang, up 10 rupiah (0.004 cent) from last week.
The benchmark December futures closed at $1,367 per tonne in New York on Tuesday. Sulawesi cocoa export prices usually trade at a $160/tonne discount to the New York price.
The discount had narrowed to around $145/tonne on Wednesday due in part to tight supply, traders said.
They said that strong demand by local grinders, mostly based in Jakarta, was also helping to keep prices steady.
"Local grinders are willing to pay a premium for local beans," one trader said. "Farmers and collectors (middlemen) are more keen on selling to the grinders than export."
He said the robust local demand has led to a dwindling of the number of exporters based in Ujung Pandang, the southernmost point on Sulawesi island east of Borneo.

Siswoputranto, executive director of producer group the Indonesia Cocoa Association (ICA), told Reuters domestic demand of cocoa was estimated to rise to 60,000 tonnes this year from around 55,000 tonnes in 1995.
He said local grinders usually export 50 percent of their products of cocoa butter and cocoa powder while the rest was channelled to Indonesian confectionaries.
Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country with 196 million people, is the third-largest cocoa producer after the Ivory Coast and Ghana.

Traders said the mid-crop harvest, which will stretch to December, was expected to produce about 40,000 tonnes of beans. They estimated 1996 total national production at 260,000-270,000 tonnes, against the ICA forecast of 290,000 tonnes.
"There are several factors to consider, including the progressing age of trees, how they are nurtured and the impact of the pod borer pest," one trader said.
Another trader said that although the pest was present in some parts of South Sulawesi, its impact on production was not significant.
